what_its_for: Captopril is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension), heart failure, and kidney problems caused by diabetes. It works by relaxing your blood vessels so your heart does not have to work as hard to pump blood.
how_to_take: Take captopril by mouth, usually 2 to 3 times a day. Take it on an EMPTY STOMACH, at least 1 hour before meals or 2 hours after meals, because food can reduce how well it works. Swallow the tablet whole or you may crush it and mix with water if you have trouble swallowing. Try to take it at the same times every day to keep a steady level in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition. Common starting doses for high blood pressure are 12.5 mg to 25 mg taken 2 to 3 times daily. For heart failure, doses often start at 6.25 mg to 12.5 mg taken 3 times daily. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over several weeks. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store captopril at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid using salt substitutes or potassium supplements unless your doctor tells you it is okay, because captopril can raise potassium levels in your blood to dangerous levels. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and cause dizziness or fainting. Be careful when standing up quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can cause dizziness. Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink enough fluids, especially in hot weather or during exercise. Tell your doctor before taking NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) as they can reduce how well captopril works and may harm your kidneys.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (this could be a serious allergic reaction called angioedema); difficulty breathing or swallowing; a severe skin rash; signs of high potassium such as muscle weakness or irregular heartbeat; signs of kidney problems such as little or no urination; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); or if you feel faint or dizzy. Also call your doctor if you develop a persistent dry cough, which is a common side effect of this medicine.
when_it_works: Captopril starts lowering your blood pressure within 1 to 2 hours after your first dose. However, it may take several weeks of regular use to see the full benefit of this medication. It is important to keep taking it even if you feel well, because high blood pressure often has no symptoms.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Do NOT take captopril if you are pregnant, especially during the second or third trimester, as it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant while taking this medicine. BREASTFEEDING: Captopril passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. ELDERLY: Older adults may be more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering effects of captopril and may have a higher risk of dizziness and falls. KIDNEY DISEASE: Your doctor may need to lower your dose if you have kidney problems, as captopril is removed from the body by the kidneys. CHILDREN: Use in children is determined by a doctor based on weight and condition.
